newsitem.title: MEXICO: Opposition gangs up on Mexico's PRI over taxes.
newsitem.headline: Opposition gangs up on Mexico's PRI over taxes.

text.p: Mexico's opposition parties, emboldened by last week's election, ganged up on the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) on Monday, vowing to overturn its unpopular tax policy.

The conservative National Action Party (PAN) and the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) said they would join forces to lower a controversial sales tax introduced two years ago by President Ernesto Zedillo.
Saul Escobar Toledo, the PRD spokesman on tax policy in Congress, told Reuters the opposition was forming a "common front" against the PRI and Zedillo's government on the issue.
In its worst electoral setback in seven decades on July 6, the PRI lost the absolute majority it has held in the lower house of Congress ever since the party was founded in 1929.
"Taxes, that's where the battle is going to be," Jorge Padilla, a PAN member of the Chamber of Deputies Finance Committee, told Reuters. "The real importance of it is to give a blow to the PRI."
Both the PAN and the PRD pledged to lower sales taxes during the mid-term election campaign, challenging Zedillo's commitment to balanced books and fiscal austerity.
According to results released on Sunday, the PRI won 239 seats in the 500-seat house, the PRD came in a surprising second with 125 deputies, and the PAN third with 122 seats.
Any tax cuts pushed through by the opposition, however, are unlikely to pass the Senate, which the PRI still controls.
By throwing down the gauntlet on taxes, the opposition hoped to hit the PRI where it was most vulnerable.

During a wrenching economic crisis in 1995, the PRI voted almost unanimously to raise the Value Added Tax to 15 from 10 percent, supporting a government austerity programme that was approved by the International Monetary Fund.
The tax hike, during the country's worst recession in 50 years, was considered a kick in the teeth by most Mexicans.

Images of PRI party leaders laughing and punching the air as they rammed the tax hike through Congress were used by the opposition as campaign propaganda and may have contributed to the ruling party's poor performance at the ballot box.
The two main opposition parties do not see eye to eye on tax policy and fissures could emerge in their common front.

In its proposal for a comprehensive reform of the tax system, the PRD is calling for new taxes on luxury goods like smoked salmon and caviar that may be resented by some of the better-heeled PAN supporters.
The PRD also objects to parts of the PAN's tax platform.
The PAN was more conciliatory. "The PRD is not bad. I think we can make a common proposal," the PAN's Padilla said.
Even if the tax cuts are voted out by the Senate, Padilla said this would still be a victory for the opposition because the PRI would be forced to block a widely popular initiative.
